strengths: The problem has an identifiable audience: researchers studying costly multi-objective experiments who need approximate Pareto-set coverage with confidence guarantees. Adaptive discretization is a useful approach to handling continuous design spaces.

The algorithm combines posterior uncertainty, bounds on within-cell variation, and inherited confidence rectangles in an understandable framework. The information-gain and metric-dimension analyses offer useful perspectives on accuracy, smoothness, and design geometry.

The experiments examine squared-exponential and Matérn kernels in one and two input dimensions, use complementary performance metrics, and include hypervolume results averaged over ten runs. The depth ablation exposes a substantial computational tradeoff, and implementation code is linked.
weaknesses: Necessary: Resolve tie handling in Definition 10 and the termination proof. Weak dominance excludes both nodes when their pessimistic vectors coincide. For example, consider rectangles with lower corners (1,1), (1,1), and (0,0), coordinate widths 0.01, and ε=(0.1,0.1). The pessimistic set is empty, so nothing is discarded; the third node remains undecided despite every diameter being below 0.1. Lemma 3's argument therefore needs an explicit treatment of ties, which the assumptions do not exclude.

Necessary: Repair the confidence calibration and dimension-bound proof. In Lemma 14, inequalities (32) and (34) reuse the parent's refinement condition at a later time. That condition need not persist because βτ increases, even though posterior variance decreases. An argument using inherited cumulative rectangles could potentially repair this step. Corollary 1 also defines V0 through log(0), and its displayed Vh contains h log N whereas substituting the specified u into 2u gives 2h log N. These issues leave Theorem 1's stated high-probability guarantee insufficiently established.

Necessary: Correct or replace Example 1. The lower bound on page 20 is T times a coefficient involving the amplitudes at index T; those amplitudes may approach zero, so the displayed bound does not imply Ω(T). Keeping the independent bump amplitudes bounded away from zero instead creates infinitely many uniformly separated points in the GP metric, incompatible with compactness and Assumption 1's Hölder comparison. The example consequently does not establish the claimed separation between the two bounds.

Necessary: Align empirical validation with the formal accuracy criterion. Sections 6.1.2–6.1.3 describe nearest-point distances with tolerance 2ε, while Definitions 3–5 require slab membership and one-sided ε-coverage. These are not interchangeable. Likewise, input-space grid spacing below ε/10 alone does not establish an objective-space approximation error. Give precise metric formulas and justify the discretization, or describe the reported ratios as approximate empirical proxies rather than validation of the formal guarantee.

Necessary: Narrow unsupported performance claims and clarify experimental configurations. The introduction claims improvements over ε-PAL, but Section 6 compares against PESMO, ParEGO, and USeMO; supply that comparison or remove the claim. Restrict broader conclusions to the synthetic settings tested. Report observation-noise variance and the depth/confidence settings used in each setup. Although the reduced-depth heuristic is disclosed, its one-minute runtime uses Vh=0, whereas the theoretical-depth configuration takes over fifteen hours; the heuristic results cannot establish the guaranteed algorithm's practical efficiency.

Optional: Experiments explicitly varying cross-objective correlation or kernel misspecification would clarify practical scope. Shortening the lengthy related-work exposition and enlarging plot legends would also improve accessibility.
